The job

Design the first Squad+ experience for US teens (13–17): onboarding (feature screens, a 13+ gate, "why are you here?") → paywall A/B → Home → one generative AI feature, as a working build on a phone.

Insight

A quiet squad feels dead. Teens pay for what makes it feel alive.

Free vs Squad+

Free: 5 people. Squad+: 12 people, premium fun and one AI feature.

Price

$3.99/week or $29.99/year, 3-day free trial.

How we got there

Question → answer → source

User

RQ1What makes a group feel alive?

Found

Small daily rituals: streaks, one daily prompt, a Home Screen widget. But they backfire when they feel forced.

  • DeskBits of Freedom survey (ages 13–21): 86% keep streaks, 42% would remove them. ↗
  • CompetitorsBeReal breaks silence with a daily prompt, Locket with a widget; BeReal later lost users. ↗

RQ2What do teens pay for?

Found

Fun, early features, AI tools, and things they don't want to lose (streaks).

  • DeskSnap: 30M subscribers; the AI/AR tier Lens+ grew ~600% this year. ↗
  • Desk25% of young streak users paid €0.99 to restore a broken streak. ↗

Onboarding

RQ3How do competitors show value before paying?

Found

Only Locket shows the benefit before sign-up; Locket and BeReal explain empty screens, with no paywall in the core flow.

  • CompetitorsCompetitor matrix: Locket shows the widget before sign-up; BeReal's first screen is just a logo, Snapchat's just sign-in buttons.
  • DeskPartiful lets guests RSVP without an account. ↗

RQ4Does a new user join by invite, or start their own squad?

Assumed

Unknown. Assumption A1: most arrive by invite; a "create + invite" flow for the rest.

  • CompanyAsk the company.
  • CompetitorsBeReal invites via QR, link and "skip".

Paywall

RQ5Weekly or annual, and how many pay after the trial?

Found

Most pick weekly, but annual subscribers stay; nearly half of trials cancel on day one.

  • DeskAdapty: 62% of revenue is weekly; 44% of trials cancel in 24h. ↗
  • DeskRevenueCat: year-one retention 44% annual vs 3% weekly. ↗

RQ6Can an under-18 pay alone?

Partial

Often not: with Ask to Buy on, a parent must approve. How it works with trials is unclear.

  • DeskApple Support: approval required; unanswered requests expire in 24h. ↗

AI

RQ7When does AI feel creepy?

Found

When it knows something it shouldn't, asks about people in photos, or can't be turned off.

  • DeskSnapchat My AI coverage: location, photo questions, can't remove it. ↗
  • DeskCommon Sense: 1 in 3 teen AI users felt uncomfortable. ↗

RQ8What data can the AI see?

Assumed

Unknown. Assumption A3: only the squad chat it's on in; no DMs, location or faces; visible to all.

  • CompanyAsk the company.

RQ9What does AI do in apps like this?

Found

Three ways: a bot in the chat (risky), creating fun content, and private catch-up summaries.

  • DeskDiscord shut down its chat bot Clyde in 2023 after offensive replies. ↗
  • DeskApple Genmoji makes an emoji from a typed description. ↗
  • DeskWhatsApp summarises unread messages; off by default, only you see it. ↗

Home

RQ10What should a new user see on Home?

Found

One next step, why an empty area is empty, and the squad itself.

  • CompetitorsCompetitor matrix: Locket and BeReal explain empty screens and show one step.
  • DeskOn BeReal you can't see friends' posts until you post yours. ↗
  • DeskGeneva splits a group into chat, audio and video rooms. ↗

RQ11When does an app or AI feel spammy?

Found

When it comes too often, sits above friends, and can't be removed.

  • DeskCommon Sense: half of teens 11–17 get 237+ notifications a day. ↗
  • DeskSnapchat's pinned, unremovable My AI got 75% one-star reviews. ↗
  • CompetitorsCompetitor matrix: BeReal ties notifications to one daily moment; Snapchat asks mid sign-up, before any value.

Extra findings

UsageTeens lead with YouTube, TikTok, Instagram and Snapchat; 36% are almost constantly online (Pew).
Sign-upAll three competitors put sign-up inside onboarding.
PaywallLocket Gold opens on a locked feature, closes with "No thanks", pre-selects annual shown monthly ($2.99/mo). Snapchat+ shows no price on its first screen.
PremiumAssumption A2: themes, effects, games, 12 people, AI; we create the brand.
AgeThe FTC asks for a neutral age screen (never pre-filled at 13+), before collecting personal data. Apple's Declared Age Range API gives an age range where the law requires it.
BenchmarkNo numbers of our own; industry paywall → paid 2.75%, trial → paid 26% (Adapty).

Problem

A new teen lands in a quiet squad and sees no reason to pay for Squad+. The known ways to break the silence backfire when forced.

Four problems

P1 · Silence

A quiet or empty squad feels dead.

86% of teens keep streaks (daily messaging runs), but 42% would remove them.

RQ1 · RQ10 · Found

P2 · Value and timing

We ask for money before value is felt.

Teens pay for fun and AI, not 12 seats; 44% of trials cancel on day one.

RQ2 · RQ3 · RQ5 · Found

P3 · AI trust and spam

AI can feel like a watcher or spam.

Snapchat's pinned, unremovable My AI got 75% one-star reviews.

RQ7 · RQ9 · RQ11 · Found · RQ8 Assumed

P4 · Teen purchase

A teen may need a parent's OK.

With Ask to Buy, a parent must approve; requests expire in 24h.

RQ6 · Partial

Assumptions · to confirm with the company

A1 · RQ4

Most users arrive by invite into an existing squad.

A2 · Premium

Premium fun = themes, effects, games. In the app: focus, study and game rooms; a plain hangout stays free.

A3 · RQ8

AI sees only that squad chat; everyone sees it, anyone can turn it off.

How might we

HMW1make a squad feel alive in 2 minutes, without pressure?
HMW2let teens feel Squad+ before we ask for money?
HMW3make the AI feel like a fun squad member, not a watcher?
HMW4keep a teen moving while a parent approves?

Solution

Show the squad alive first, ask for money second; one AI spark a day brings a quiet squad back.

13+ gate (at sign-in)→Feature screens→What are you here for?→Paywall A/B→Home→Spark

The age gate comes first, not third: a teen under 13 should not see the product pitch, and the FTC asks for the age screen before any personal data.

Key idea · S1 · AI feature · HMW3

Squad Spark: when the chat goes quiet, one spark a day gets the squad talking.

What it does

Leaves one "spark" in the squad chat: a question, a mini game or a photo task. "Drop this week's funniest moment", "Who wakes up first? Vote".

When

Only after the chat has been quiet for a while; at most once a day. Never in a live squad.

State 1 · the member who turns it on

Picks a vibe and sees Spark's four rules before adding it (needs Squad+).

State 2 · the rest of the squad

Sees "Maya added Spark" with Mute, and the spark inside their squad's card on Home.

💬Reads only this chat
✕No DMs, faces or location
🔔Max once a day, when quiet
🔕Anyone can mute or remove it

Not a streak: no counter, nothing to lose if you skip it. Two sparks in a row with no answer and it takes a break. Why: My AI backlash and notification overload (RQ7, RQ11); daily rituals work but backfire when forced (RQ1).

What we design

S2 · Feature screens · HMW2

A live squad preview before any ask.

Three swipeable pages, one graphic and one idea each: your squad is already talking, rooms to hang out, focus and play in, and Spark so the chat never dies. Locket shows value before sign-up.

S3 · What are you here for? · HMW1

One tap: hang out, study, share moments.

Personalises the paywall's headline and art.

S4 · Paywall A / B · HMW2

Two paywalls: A fun and AI, B the squad (12 seats).

A leads with what they came for. Annual pre-selected, shown monthly, clear close (like Locket Gold). Metric: day-7 paid conversion per paywall view.

S5 · Home · HMW1

Who's here, today's spark, one next step.

Live squads first: who's here and the room friends started (join it or start your own). Quiet squads below, with Spark's spark inside their card. If empty: why + invite (RQ10). No streaks.

S6 · Ask a parent · HMW4

"Waiting for approval"; keep using free meanwhile.

Ask to Buy can take up to 24h.

Experiment note · Paywall A vs B

Where it runs. The paywall at the end of onboarding, for new users who joined by invite. Split 50/50 by account, sticky; same plans (yearly pre-selected, shown per month), same 3-day trial, same "No thanks".

A (control) · fun and AI. Headline and art follow their answer ("Play more, together." with a game room, "Study together, for real." with a focus room).

B (variant) · the squad. "Room for 12." 5 of 5 seats taken, 7 empty, and two friends who asked to join ("Sam and Priya want in"). No contact list needed: they are friends who tapped the squad's invite.

Hypothesis. B beats A on day-7 paid conversion per paywall view because a teen who arrives by invite (A1) already feels the table is full: friends who can't get in is a reason they get on day one; features they haven't used aren't. Our research says the opposite (teens pay for fun and AI), so it's a real bet.

Deciding metric. Day-7 paid conversion per paywall view: trials that become paid, approved Ask to Buy requests included. Day 7, not day 3, so a parent's 24 h approval and early refunds count. Trial starts alone would reward pressure (44% cancel in 24 h). ~15,200 views per arm to see a +20% lift (2.75% → 3.30%); two to four weeks.

Side effects to watch. Ask to Buy decline rate; refunds; plan mix (yearly vs weekly); invites sent; day-7 activity of users who said no.

Stop early if B's Ask to Buy declines run 5+ points above A's, refunds double, anyone reports the friends B names, or the 50/50 split drifts (broken tracking).

Next test. B wins: show the seat moment on Home when a squad fills, before any paywall. B loses: keep A and test Spark's first spark inside the paywall.

Test plan · how we would run it

How we would run the experiment in the note, step by step. Numbers are planning assumptions until we have our own baseline.

1. Before launch

  • Write it down first. Hypothesis, the one deciding metric, guardrails, sample size, stop date and decision rule are fixed before the first user sees B. No new success metric after the fact.
  • Who is in. New users who joined by invite and reach the paywall at the end of onboarding. Users who start their own table are out: B's "5 of 5 seats taken" isn't true for them.
  • How they're split. 50/50 by account at the first paywall view, and sticky: a user sees the same paywall every time. Both arms sell the same two products ($3.99/week, $29.99/year, 3-day trial); only the screen changes. Run it with RevenueCat Experiments (two Offerings on the same placement) or a remote feature flag.
  • QA both arms on a real iPhone, including the under-18 Ask to Buy path, and check that every event (paywall view, trial start, paid, refund) arrives once per user.

2. Sample size and length

Baseline2.75% paywall view → paid (industry, Adapty)
Smallest lift worth shipping+20% relative (2.75% → 3.30%)
Significance / power5% two-sided / 80%
Sample~15,200 paywall views per arm (~30,500 total)
Enrolmentat least 14 days (two full weeks, weekday and weekend), at most 28
Read-out7 days after the last user enrols (3-day trial + 24 h Ask to Buy + early refunds)

If 28 days can't reach the sample, we don't run longer: we accept a bigger lift (+30% needs ~7,100 per arm) or stop the test.

3. While it runs

  • No peeking at the winner. We read the deciding metric once, at the planned end. Looking every day and stopping when it "looks significant" turns a 5% false-positive rate into 25% or more.
  • Daily health checks only:
    • Split: a sample-ratio mismatch (chi-square p < 0.001) means the tracking is broken; pause and fix, and throw away the data.
    • Guardrails (stop B early if it crosses one): Ask to Buy declines 5+ points above A, refunds double A's, or any report about the friends B names.

4. Reading the result

  1. Check the split again (SRM).
  2. Deciding metric: day-7 paid conversion per paywall view, compared with a two-proportion test.
  3. Pre-planned cuts (to explain, not to pick a winner): under 18 vs 18+ (Ask to Buy), yearly vs weekly mix.
  4. Secondary: trial starts, invites sent, day-7 activity of users who said no.

5. Decision

ResultWhat we do
B wins, guardrails fineShip B to invited users. Next: test the seat moment on Home, before any paywall.
No significant differenceKeep A (it matches our research and is simpler).
B loses, or a guardrail firesKeep A. Next: test Spark's first spark inside the paywall.

B changes several things at once (headline, art, named friends, button text), so a win tells us "seats beat fun", not which part did it. The follow-up test isolates the named friends.

Sources accessed 9 Nov 2026. A1–A3 are our assumptions, to confirm with the company. Screenshots from the iOS build, 13 Nov 2026.
